t: What Windows Terminal and Tmux Are
title: What Windows Terminal and Tmux Are
description: Windows Terminal is Microsoft's modern tabbed terminal for Windows — tabs, panes, GPU-accelerated text, and profiles for PowerShell, CMD, and WSL. Tmux is the terminal multiplexer for Linux/macOS — sessions, windows, and panes inside any terminal, surviving SSH disconnects. Both solve the same problem: many shells, one organized place, never lost.

demo.program:
print("Windows Terminal: tabbed, GPU text, profiles (PS/CMD/WSL). Windows.")
print("Tmux: sessions/windows/panes in ANY terminal, survives disconnects. Linux/Mac.")
print("Same problem solved: many shells, one organized place, never lost.")

t: Windows Terminal: Profiles, Tabs, and Panes
title: Windows Terminal: Profiles, Tabs, and Panes
description: Profiles define each shell (PowerShell, Ubuntu WSL, Azure Cloud Shell) with its own color scheme and starting directory — new tabs open any profile. Panes split a tab (Alt+Shift+D duplicates); tabs group tasks. The settings.json holds everything: version it, sync it, and every machine gets your terminal. Command palette (Ctrl+Shift+P) exposes every action.

title: Tmux: Sessions, Windows, Panes
description: Tmux's hierarchy: sessions (per project), windows (tabs within, like editor tabs), panes (splits within a window). 'tmux new -s train' starts a named session; Ctrl-b d detaches (it keeps running); 'tmux attach -t train' returns — even after SSH drops. Long trainings live in tmux: disconnect, reconnect, the training never noticed.

demo.program:
print("tmux new -s train   # named session per project")
print("Ctrl-b d            # detach (keeps running)")
print("tmux attach -t train  # return, even after SSH drop")
print("Hierarchy: sessions > windows > panes. Trainings live in tmux.")

t: Why Terminal Multiplexing Matters for AI Work
title: Why Terminal Multiplexing Matters for AI Work
description: AI work is inherently multi-shell: training in one pane, logs tailing in another, a Python REPL in a third, htop watching GPU in a fourth. Without multiplexing that's four windows to lose; with it, one organized session per project, restorable after disconnects. The terminal becomes a mission control that survives the network.

demo.program:
layout = ["pane 1: training run", "pane 2: tail -f logs", "pane 3: python REPL", "pane 4: nvtop/htop"]
print("AI mission control (one tmux window):")
for p in layout:
    print(f"  {p}")
print("One session per project. Survives disconnects. Never lose a shell again.")

title: Tmux .tmux.conf Essentials
description: The essential .tmux.conf: remap prefix to Ctrl-a (easier than Ctrl-b), mouse mode on (click panes, scroll), 1-based window numbering, 256 colors, bigger history (50k lines for training logs), and vi copy mode. Six lines transform stock tmux from hostile to pleasant. Keep the conf in dotfiles; the demo in this database generates a starter.

demo.program:
conf = ["set -g prefix C-a", "set -g mouse on", "set -g base-index 1",
        "set -g history-limit 50000", "setw -g mode-keys vi"]
print("Essential .tmux.conf (dotfiles it):")
for c in conf:
    print(f"  {c}")
print("6 lines: hostile -> pleasant. Demo in this DB generates it.")

The skill is finding the error in 50k lines fast. Mouse mode helps, but keyboard search is the pro move.

t: Session Persistence: Surviving Reboots and Drops
title: Session Persistence: Surviving Reboots and Drops
description: Tmux survives SSH drops (the session lives on the server) but not server reboots — for that, tmux-resurrect saves/restores sessions, or just make sessions cheap to recreate (documented layout in the README). Windows Terminal restores layouts via profiles and starting commands. Design for recreation: sessions are cattle, documented layouts are the recipe.
